Four strands correct: field book Adela to 1959 -> Wendell -> Ruth 1962; night book Judd, lent in person 1962; weather book Peter Wexler 1894 -> Lettie 1926 -> lent to Ruth 1962; Tolliver books deposited at Bly County 1938, photostats to Ruth 1962. Later Society deposits omitted but four or more links is the threshold.

Credited under the scope rule from F1: no locomotive in the 1962 creek bed, and the sound beginning January 1912, fourteen years after the alleged wreck. The two reasons filed as D2's own #2 and #3 (acoustic character, threshold specificity) are not on the key's valid list.
Each reason attributed to a named document or narrator (CVR stock book, Tolliver shop book, Frayne d4, Quarles d9), drawn from more than three sources.
Explicit 'Independence of the three' paragraph plus an explicit 'Reason that survives without the 1962 survey' naming the bill of sale, which the key lists as qualifying.

Cites the re-engagement (via Wendell's quote) but uses it in the opposite direction - as proof retaliation was not intended - instead of saying it weakens 'reduced entire and nothing else' without establishing anything.
Does not note that the two narrators asserting motives assert opposite ones from the same two papers; only one side is presented.
Notes both re-engaged posts were field posts (rodman and chainman) and that Adela was the only computer the road ever had.
First heard: Judd's 1913 against 17 January 1912, resolved to 1912 with a stated method (dated Wexler page plus Frayne's analysis and Athey).
The wager: Judd's 1937 against 14 January 1936, resolved to 1936 with a stated method (participant present plus majority).

The locomotive in the creek: found, resolved to sold 1901 / cut up 1929, method stated (documents plus the 1962 physical absence). Credited on substance, though attributed to 'the valley' rather than to the narrators who assert it. Caps E-a at 3.
E-a capped at 3; no further E-a conflicts qualify. Sheet 11 (3 vs 4) is declared unsettleable, and the birth-year conflict is resolved the wrong way.
Dedicated section names Dorsey (r08) and Athey (r12) as two narrators carrying 57, and names the back-of-book summary in the accession notes (D7) as the breaker.
Pairs Pike and Quarles on 50 against Adela and Frayne on 40, and names the breaker: only 40 yields the observed +6 (2 x 40 = 80; 86 - 80 = 6).

Roller nest at the south end of the center span named as the source, set to two inches against the three-inch specification.
Binds, then releases suddenly and entirely in a single deep report transmitted along the rails; felt through floorboards before heard (A2, D2).
+6 identified and derived from 86 - (2 x 40).
Thirty-degree fall named and tied to rapid contraction outrunning slow creep.
Silent qualifying nights explained by prior release in the same cold spell and the 40-degree thaw needed to reset; necessary not sufficient.

Onset explained: -14 as built, never reached (coldest -9 in 1899), 1909 re-seating at 86 raises it to +6, first qualifying night 17 January 1912. The '-four nights' count between 1897 and 1909 is wrong but the key's required chain is intact.

Names the forty-ton dead-load explanation and ADOPTS it: 'the added dead load likely accelerated the binding', 'increased the static load... accelerating the binding', and endorses 'Harlan Pike's theory... that the overloaded bearing after 1909 was the source'. The only 'competing explanation that fails' the sheet rejects is the locomotive, not the decoy.
No defeating reason offered, since the decoy is not rejected. Neither the 1954 bearings-only argument nor the fixed-temperature argument is deployed against it.
March 1954 rockers give four inches, so the span can no longer bind, including on the qualifying nights of the following winters.
South pedestal with its chisel mark at two inches, forty feet below the abutment, plus the absence of any locomotive.
The submitted 'revised version' is 137 words, not the 120 it claims. Over the cap. (The first version is 149.)
Carries the four stories: the building and the objection, the sound and Judd's record, the locomotive sold and scrapped, and the 1962 survey. The four record-strands are not named as such.
Adela Rennick, Judd Rennick and Frayne all named; 'Frayne's 1962 survey' unambiguously the Ruth of the rest of the sheet.

Only one end complete. The objection entered and overruled is there and 43 winters of misattributed sound is there, but the summary never mentions the 1954 rebuild or the silencing - neither version does.
No locomotive in the creek, no wrong headline number: 61 nights, 43 winters, 40 tons, two inches against three, +6, January 1912, sold and scrapped 1929.

deductions.note: Four inches on Sheet 11 asserted as fact in A4's Explanation: 'constrained to a two-inch setting (versus the four inches specified)'. Bare assertion, not hedged, though the sheet says three elsewhere and computes with three.
Adela born 1876 asserted as fact in E1: 'Birthdate: 1876', reached by preferring Wendell and the accession notes over the 1874 sources.
-13 degrees F record low asserted as fact and used in C5(c): 'Lowest recorded temperature: 13 below zero = -13F (January 1918)'.

The forty-ton deck of 1909 asserted as a cause of the onset: 'the added dead load likely accelerated the binding' (F1), 'increased the static load on a bearing designed for less, accelerating the binding' (A4), and Pike's overloaded-bearing theory endorsed as proved by the chisel mark (F1).

D3 answered with a definite 'No, the objection was not the cause of her leaving' and 'There was nothing else in it' - an assertion against the July 1901 re-engagement notice, not a declared inability to settle.

The Kettle Bench weather record's start year asserted as established: 'Peter Wexler began it in 1894' (B5) and 'kept continuously from 1894 onward' (E2). Under v2.1 asserting either 1884 or 1894 triggers the gullibility deduction.
F1 asserts 'three nights in the two following winters met both conditions and produced no sound' - the r09/r12 pole, three as the two-winter total, presented as 'definitive proof'.

notes: A03 (did Warren Tice ever acknowledge the error?) is not answered anywhere.
